name: Passionflower
description: A sprawling vine of the American Southeast whose otherworldly purple-fringed blooms look like small clockwork mandalas. Spanish missionaries read the Passion of Christ into its parts, the corona as the crown of thorns and the stamens as the wounds, and named it accordingly. The Cherokee and other Native peoples ate the egg-shaped 'maypop' fruits long before then and used the vine as a gentle calming medicine.
metaphysicalUses: Passionflower is an herb of peace. Placed in the home, it calms quarrels and soothes the troubles that hang about a household. Folk practice tucks it under the pillow so you sleep without fretting, and carries it to attract friends and kindly regard. Its spiralling, many-pointed flower makes a natural focus for meditation, and it suits rituals for emotional healing, coming down after a crisis, and calming an overactive mind before divination. Add it to peace sachets, sleep pillows and reconciliation jars, or float the flowers in a bowl of moon water on the altar.
medicalUses: In Western and Native American herbalism, passionflower is a classic nervine. Folk healers have used it to quiet a racing mind, ease nervous restlessness and help people fall asleep, especially when worry keeps them awake. Herbalists usually give it as a tea or tincture of the dried aerial parts, often with lemon balm, skullcap or chamomile. It was also used for nervous headaches and tension in the muscles.
whereToFind: Native to the southeastern United States, where it rambles over fences, field edges, roadsides and sunny thickets. It is hardy to about zone 6 and easy to grow from seed or cuttings on a trellis in full sun. Gather leaves and flowers in summer while it blooms, and the fruits once they turn yellow and wrinkle. Dried herb is sold at apothecaries, herb shops and online herbal suppliers.
uses: Hang a sprig of dried passionflower over the bedroom door to calm a restless household
Stuff a dream pillow with passionflower, lavender and hops for peaceful sleep
Gaze into a fresh bloom as a natural mandala before meditation
Add to a reconciliation jar with sugar and rose petals to soothe a quarrel
Brew a calming evening tea of passionflower and lemon balm
Carry the dried flower in a blue sachet to draw new friends
Grow the vine on a garden arch to invite peace into the home
caution: Can cause drowsiness, dizziness and confusion; do not drive after taking it. Do not use during pregnancy, since it may cause uterine contractions, and little is known about safety while breastfeeding. Stop at least 2 weeks before surgery. Use only Passiflora incarnata, because some other Passiflora species contain cyanogenic compounds. Short-term use only (tea up to about a week, extracts up to about 8 weeks) unless a healthcare provider advises otherwise.
interactions: Adds to the effects of sedatives, sleep aids, benzodiazepines, anesthesia, opioids and alcohol. Use caution with antidepressants and other drugs that affect the nervous system.

name: Skullcap
description: A modest mint-family plant of damp woodland edges. Its little blue flowers wear a tiny cap or helmet on the calyx, which gives it its name. Eighteenth-century American doctors once promoted it as a cure for rabies, so it is still called 'mad dog' skullcap. Today it is valued above all as a friend to frayed nerves.
metaphysicalUses: Skullcap is an herb of peace, relaxation and loyalty. Cunningham records an old custom: a wife carries skullcap so that her husband will not be charmed away by other women, which makes it a quiet ally in fidelity and commitment work. It is added to spells for calm and to meditation blends that help a scattered mind settle and focus inward. Some practitioners use it in gentle binding work, to stop one's own anxious thoughts rather than to bind another. Burn a pinch with lavender or place it in charm bags carried during stressful times.
medicalUses: Traditional Western herbalism counts skullcap among the finest nervine tonics. It was used to soothe frayed nerves, ease nervous exhaustion, tension headaches and restless sleep, and to steady people through emotional upheaval. Folk herbalists prefer the fresh plant tincture or a tea of the dried herb, often blended with oats, passionflower or chamomile.
whereToFind: Native to North America, growing in wet meadows, along streams and riverbanks, in marshes and in moist woodland clearings. It grows easily from seed in partial shade with rich, moist soil. Harvest the aerial parts while in flower in mid to late summer. Buy from reputable herbal suppliers, because commercial skullcap has historically been adulterated with toxic germander (Teucrium).
uses: Carry a sachet of skullcap to strengthen loyalty and commitment in a partnership
Add to a meditation blend with lavender to quiet a chattering mind
Brew a cup of skullcap and oatstraw tea after a draining day
Place under the pillow alongside a written worry, to be released by morning
Sprinkle in the corners of a room after an argument to restore calm
Include in fidelity spells and handfasting charms
caution: May cause drowsiness; avoid driving until you know how it affects you, and avoid alcohol. Not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, some linked to products adulterated with germander, so buy third-party tested products that name the species, avoid it with liver disease, and stop if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or pale stools. People allergic to mint-family plants should avoid it. Consult a healthcare provider before use.
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives, sleep, pain and anxiety medicines and alcohol. Discuss with a provider if you take blood thinners, statins or other drugs that affect the liver.

name: Hops
description: A vigorous climbing bine whose papery, pale-green cones carry a golden, resinous dust called lupulin. Pliny called it 'willow wolf' because it smothered the trees it climbed. Since the Middle Ages it has flavoured and preserved beer. Hop pickers were said to grow drowsy in the fields, and the hop pillow became a famous cure for sleeplessness. King George III is said to have slept on one.
metaphysicalUses: Hops is above all an herb of sleep and healing. Fill a small pillow with dried hops, or hops mixed with lavender, to bring restful, untroubled slumber and calm dreams. It is used in healing incenses and sachets and can be added to charms that soothe nightmares. Because of its link with brewing, hops also belongs in harvest celebrations and Lammas or Mabon rites honouring the grain and the brewer's craft. Hanging a garland of hop bines over the hearth was an old way to welcome the bounty of autumn.
medicalUses: Hops has long been used in folk medicine as a sedative and bitter tonic. A hop pillow or hop tea was the old country remedy for sleeplessness and nervous restlessness. As a bitter, it was taken to stimulate appetite and digestion and to ease nervous indigestion. Herbalists combine it with valerian and passionflower in sleep blends.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and North America, it grows wild in hedgerows, thickets and damp woodland edges, and is cultivated in hop yards. Plant rhizomes in spring in full sun with a tall support; the bines can climb 6 m in a season. Harvest the cones in late summer when they feel papery and leave yellow lupulin on the fingers. Dried hops are sold by homebrew shops, herb suppliers and apothecaries.
uses: Stitch a hop pillow to banish insomnia and nightmares
Hang a garland of hop bines over the hearth at Mabon for harvest blessings
Burn dried hops in a healing incense blend
Add to a sleep sachet with lavender and chamomile
Use in a bitter evening tea to settle a nervous stomach
Brew your own ale as a seasonal offering to the land spirits
caution: Sedating; avoid with alcohol or sedatives and before driving. Avoid in depression and with estrogen-sensitive conditions such as some breast or uterine cancers and endometriosis, because of its phytoestrogens. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Handling fresh hops can cause skin irritation or allergy in some people. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives, sleep aids and alcohol. May interfere with estrogen or hormone therapies.
pets: Hops (fresh, dried or spent brewing hops) are poisonous to dogs and can cause a dangerous, rapid rise in body temperature (malignant hyperthermia) that can be fatal; greyhounds and retrievers seem most at risk. Get emergency veterinary care if a dog eats any.

name: Blue Lotus
folkNames: Sacred Narcotic Lily of the Nile
description: The sky-blue water lily of the Nile. It opens with the morning sun and sinks below the water at dusk, so the ancient Egyptians saw it as a symbol of creation, rebirth and the sun itself. It is painted on tomb walls, held to the noses of nobles at banquets, and was scattered over the body of Tutankhamun. In myth the god Nefertem rose from a blue lotus at the dawn of the world.
metaphysicalUses: Blue lotus is a flower of awakening, rebirth and the opening of higher consciousness. It is used in meditation and ritual to lift the spirit, in dreamwork and lucid dreaming, and for devotion to the Egyptian gods, especially Nefertem, Ra and Isis. Its petals are placed on the altar, steeped in ritual bath water or anointing waters, or burned in sacred incense. Because the flower rises clean and radiant from the mud, it is a powerful image for transformation, purity and new beginnings after hardship. It is also used in love and sensuality rites, recalling its place at Egyptian banquets.
medicalUses: Historically it was steeped in wine or water in Egypt and inhaled as a perfume for gentle euphoria and relaxation. In modern folk use the dried flowers are made into a mild tea or smoked for calm, dreamy relaxation and as a sleep aid. Scientific evidence is limited and the plant contains psychoactive alkaloids (aporphine, nuciferine), so treat it with care.
whereToFind: Native to the Nile and parts of East Africa, it grows in still, warm, shallow water. It can be grown in tropical ponds or large water tubs in warm climates, wintering indoors elsewhere. Dried flowers and petals are sold by specialist herb and ethnobotanical suppliers. Check local laws, since some regions restrict its sale for consumption.
uses: Float dried petals in a ritual bath before meditation or devotion
Place a blue lotus on the altar as an offering to Isis or Nefertem
Add petals to a dream pillow for vivid, lucid dreams
Burn petals with frankincense in an Egyptian-style temple incense
Meditate on the image of the lotus rising from the mud during shadow work
Infuse petals in moon water for anointing third-eye work
caution: Mildly psychoactive; high doses can cause dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, agitation, nausea, fast heartbeat, hallucinations and poor balance. It is not approved by the FDA as a food or supplement, its safety has not been studied, and products may be contaminated or spiked with synthetic cannabinoids. Do not drive after use, and avoid it during pregnancy and breastfeeding, in children, and with liver disease. Legal status varies by place. Do not smoke or vape it; if burning petals as incense, use a fireproof dish and ventilate.
interactions: Do not combine with alcohol, sedatives, pain or anxiety medicines, or other psychoactive substances (excess sedation). It may interact with drugs that affect dopamine or serotonin and with drugs processed by the same liver enzymes.
pets: Keep products away from pets; effects in animals are not well studied.

name: Violet
description: A shy, heart-leaved woodland flower with a sweet scent that famously comes and goes, because its ionone compounds briefly numb the nose. The Greeks wove violet garlands for Aphrodite and claimed Athens as the 'violet-crowned city'. Persephone was gathering violets when Hades carried her below. Napoleon's followers wore violets as their secret emblem while he was in exile.
metaphysicalUses: Violet is a gentle Venusian flower of love, modesty, peace and wishes. Carry the flowers for protection against changes in luck and to bring good fortune. Mix with lavender for a love charm that stirs gentle, faithful affection. Old lore says that seeing the first violet of spring grants a wish, and that wearing a violet garland eases a heavy heart and dispels evil spirits. Violets are loved by the faery folk and grief-healing spirits, and their crystallised flowers make sweet offerings. Sleep with the leaves in your pillow for prophetic, tender dreams, or scatter the petals to sweeten a home in mourning.
medicalUses: Culpeper considered violet a cooling, moistening plant. Its syrup was a traditional children's remedy for coughs, sore throats and chest congestion, and the leaves were made into poultices for swellings and hot inflamed skin. Folk healers applied violet leaf compresses to the forehead for headaches and used the leaves in salves for dry or irritated skin. Fresh leaves and flowers are also eaten in spring salads.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia and naturalised widely, sweet violet grows in shady hedgebanks, woodland edges, lawns and gardens, flowering in late winter and early spring. It spreads easily by runners in partial shade and moist, rich soil. Pick flowers and leaves in spring from unsprayed areas. Seeds and plants are sold at garden centers; dried leaf and flower at herb shops. Note: African violets are unrelated.
uses: Make wishes upon the first violet you find in spring
Crystallise violets in sugar as faery offerings or love-spell treats
Carry violets and lavender in a sachet to attract tender love
Stuff leaves into a dream pillow for gentle prophetic dreams
Make violet syrup with honey to soothe a cough (never give honey to babies under 1 year)
Lay violet flowers on graves or memorial altars to comfort the grieving
Wear a violet in the hair to ward off ill spirits
caution: Leaves and flowers are generally safe in food amounts. The roots and seeds are emetic and should not be eaten. Be sure of identification, and do not harvest from sprayed lawns or roadsides. Never give honey (including honey syrups) to babies under 1 year old, because of infant botulism. Avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy and breastfeeding, as safety has not been established.

name: Marjoram
description: A soft, grey-green, sweetly fragrant Mediterranean herb. Greek legend says it was created by Aphrodite as a symbol of happiness. Greek and Roman newlyweds were crowned with marjoram wreaths for joy in marriage, and the herb was planted on graves to bring the dead peaceful rest. In medieval Europe it was a favourite strewing herb that sweetened floors and chased away melancholy.
metaphysicalUses: Marjoram is an herb of joy, love and protection. Add it to love spells and sachets, and place a little in every room of the house for protection. Freshen it each month. A bunch of fresh marjoram brought to someone who is grieving or depressed is said to bring happiness. It is used in money and prosperity blends, and was traditionally woven into wedding crowns and handfasting garlands. Planting marjoram on a grave honours the dead and helps them rest. It also makes a gentle, joyful addition to home blessing washes and kitchen witchery.
medicalUses: In folk herbalism, marjoram tea has been taken to ease indigestion, gas and colic, to soothe colds and coughs, and to calm nervous tension and help sleep. Infused oil or sweet marjoram essential oil (diluted) was massaged into aching muscles, stiff joints and sore bellies during menstrual cramps. Culpeper praised it for 'all diseases of the chest' and for warming a cold stomach.
whereToFind: Native to the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia, it is widely cultivated as a culinary herb. It is tender, so grow it as an annual in cool climates, in full sun with light, well-drained soil. Harvest leaves just before flowering for best flavour. Fresh and dried marjoram are found at grocers, farmers' markets and herb suppliers; seedlings at garden centers.
uses: Place a small bowl of dried marjoram in each room for protection, refreshing monthly
Bring fresh marjoram to a grieving friend to lift their heart
Weave marjoram into a handfasting crown for joyful marriage
Add to a love sachet with rose and lavender
Sprinkle in a home blessing floor wash
Cook with marjoram while focusing on joy and harmony in the household
Massage diluted marjoram oil into sore muscles
caution: Safe in culinary amounts. Avoid medicinal doses and the essential oil during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and in young children. The essential oil must be diluted (about 1 to 3 percent in a carrier oil) before skin use, patch tested, and never ingested. People allergic to mint-family plants (oregano, basil, thyme) may react. Stop medicinal doses 2 weeks before surgery.
interactions: Medicinal amounts may slow blood clotting and lower blood sugar; use caution with blood thinners and diabetes medicines.
pets: The ASPCA lists marjoram as toxic to dogs and cats (vomiting, diarrhea). Essential oils are dangerous to cats; do not diffuse or apply them where cats live or groom.

name: Oregano
description: The robust, peppery wild cousin of sweet marjoram. Its name comes from the Greek 'oros ganos', 'joy of the mountain', for the purple-pink flowers that cover Mediterranean hillsides in summer. The Greeks believed that oregano growing on a grave meant the departed was happy in the afterlife. Grazing animals on oregano-covered hills were said to yield the sweetest meat.
metaphysicalUses: Oregano brings joy, vitality and protection. Use it to lift depression and attract happiness, to help release a former lover, and in love spells for a lighthearted, joyful romance. It can be burned or hung to protect the home, and mixed into money and luck spells. It is a natural herb of the kitchen witch: sprinkling it into food while cooking with intent brings harmony and good cheer to those who eat. Planting or placing oregano at a grave honours the dead and wishes them joy in the next world.
medicalUses: Folk medicine has long used oregano tea for coughs, colds, sore throats and indigestion, and steam inhalations to clear stuffy sinuses. Oregano is strongly antiseptic and antifungal, so poultices and well-diluted oil were applied to minor wounds, fungal skin complaints and aching joints. It is a warming, stimulating herb traditionally given at the first sign of chills.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, the Mediterranean and western Asia, it grows wild on dry, sunny, chalky hillsides, field margins and rocky slopes. It is a hardy perennial and easy to grow in full sun with lean, well-drained soil. Harvest leaves and flowering tops in midsummer. Widely available fresh, dried and as essential oil at grocers, garden centers and herb suppliers.
uses: Sprinkle oregano into family meals to bring joy and harmony to the table
Burn dried oregano to help let go of a past love
Hang a bundle in the kitchen for protection
Add to a happiness sachet with lemon balm and marjoram
Make a steam inhalation of dried oregano herb (not essential oil) for congestion
Leave a sprig on a grave to wish the departed joy
Use in luck and money powders
caution: Safe in food amounts. Oregano essential oil is a strong skin and mucous-membrane irritant: never use it undiluted, keep it at about 1 percent or less on skin, keep it away from eyes, and never ingest it without professional guidance. Use the dried herb, not the oil, for steam inhalations, keep eyes closed and do not use steam with young children. Avoid medicinal doses during pregnancy and breastfeeding. May cause reactions in people allergic to mint-family plants. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
interactions: Medicinal doses or oil may increase bleeding risk with blood thinners and may lower blood sugar with diabetes medicines.
pets: The ASPCA lists oregano as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (mild vomiting and diarrhea). Essential oils are dangerous to cats; do not diffuse or apply them where cats live or groom.

name: Parsley
description: A humble garden herb with a surprisingly dark history. The Greeks linked parsley with death, laid it on tombs and crowned victors at the funeral games of Archemorus with it. 'To be in need of parsley' meant to be near death. Folk lore says the seed goes to the Devil and back seven or nine times before it sprouts, which is why it is so slow to germinate, and that only a witch or a strong-willed woman can grow it well.
metaphysicalUses: Parsley is used for protection, purification and lust. The Romans tucked sprigs into their togas for protection, and a sprig on a plate guarded food against contamination. Ritual baths with parsley purify the body and help stop misfortune. It is used in Persephone and underworld rites and in honouring the dead. Old lore says never to cut parsley if you are in love, or you will cut your love as well. In love and lust magic, eating parsley was said to stir desire. It is also a fertility herb, sown at Good Friday for luck in the garden.
medicalUses: Traditionally parsley has been used as a diuretic and kidney tonic, to ease water retention, and as a digestive herb against bloating and wind. Chewing the fresh leaves sweetens the breath. It is rich in vitamin C and iron. Old herbals also used the bruised leaves as a poultice for bruises and insect bites.
whereToFind: Native to the central Mediterranean, it is now grown in kitchen gardens worldwide. It is a biennial; soak seeds overnight to speed their famously slow germination and sow in rich, moist soil in sun or part shade. Harvest leaves as needed. Fresh parsley is sold at every grocer; seeds and seedlings at garden centers. Never forage wild 'parsley', since deadly hemlock and fool's parsley look similar.
uses: Add parsley to a purification bath to wash away misfortune
Tuck a sprig into a pocket or purse for protection
Lay parsley on an ancestor altar or grave in honour of the dead
Garnish food with a sprig to protect it from ill intent
Sow parsley on Good Friday for garden luck
Chew fresh leaves after a meal to sweeten the breath
caution: Safe as food. Avoid medicinal amounts, seeds, concentrated juices and essential oil during pregnancy and breastfeeding, since they can stimulate the uterus; parsley seed oil (apiol) can damage the liver and kidneys. Avoid medicinal doses with kidney disease and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Never forage wild, because it resembles deadly hemlock and fool's parsley.
interactions: Large amounts may affect warfarin because of vitamin K, and may add to the effects of diuretics and lithium (by changing fluid and salt balance).
pets: The ASPCA lists parsley as toxic to dogs, cats and horses in large amounts (sun sensitivity and skin reactions).

name: Tansy
partsUsed: flowers, leaves (dried, for non-ingestive use only)
description: A tall, pungent, fern-leaved plant with flat clusters of bright yellow button flowers. Its old name 'athanasia' means 'immortality'. Greek myth tells that Zeus gave Ganymede a drink of tansy to make him immortal, and tansy was later packed into coffins and burial shrouds to deter decay and vermin. In medieval Europe tansy cakes were eaten at Easter, but today the plant is known to be toxic.
metaphysicalUses: Tansy is an herb of longevity and immortality, linked to death rites and to protecting the dead. Dried bundles are hung or placed on ancestor altars to honour those who have passed and to wish loved ones long life. It is a strong banishing and protective herb: hung by doors and windows it repels flies and other pests, both physical and spiritual. Carried in a sealed sachet it was said to protect health and lengthen life. Its golden buttons also serve as a symbol of steadfast life force in protective and healing charms.
medicalUses: Historically tansy was used as a vermifuge to expel intestinal worms, and was strewn on floors and rubbed on meat to keep insects away. These internal uses are now considered dangerous because of its thujone content. Today it is valued only externally as an insect-repelling herb in the garden and home.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia, it is naturalised and often invasive in North America, growing along roadsides, riverbanks, field edges and waste ground. It flowers from midsummer to autumn. It is a declared noxious weed in some regions, so check before planting. Wear gloves when gathering. Dried flowers are sometimes sold by herb suppliers for crafts and pest repellent.
uses: Hang dried tansy bundles by doorways to repel flies and ill spirits
Place sealed sachets of dried tansy on an ancestor altar to honour the dead
Tuck dried tansy among stored woollens to deter moths
Plant tansy at the edge of the garden as a companion to repel pests
Use the golden buttons in wreaths and dried arrangements for longevity magic
Draw or press the flower in your grimoire as a symbol of immortality
caution: POISONOUS: tansy contains thujone and is toxic if eaten or taken as tea, oil or tincture. It can cause convulsions, liver and kidney damage, miscarriage and death. Never ingest it, and never use tansy oil. Wear gloves, because it can cause skin irritation and allergic reactions, especially in people sensitive to the daisy family. Keep away from children and pets, and avoid handling it during pregnancy.
pets: Toxic to dogs, cats and livestock if eaten; keep dried bundles and sachets out of reach.

name: Feverfew
description: A bushy cottage-garden herb with lacy, sharply aromatic leaves and masses of small daisy-like flowers with fat yellow centres. Its name is a corruption of 'febrifuge', a fever-dispeller. Its species name 'parthenium' is said to honour a workman saved by it when he fell from the Parthenon. Medieval herbalists planted it near houses to purify the air and ward off disease.
metaphysicalUses: Feverfew is a protective herb. Carried, it guards against colds, fevers and accidents, especially while travelling. Old practice planted it around the house to purify the air and keep illness away, so it suits protective boundary plantings and healing gardens. Use it in charm bags for health and safe journeys, in healing incense, and in spells that 'cool' a hot situation, such as rising tempers or simmering arguments.
medicalUses: Feverfew is the classic folk remedy for headaches. Traditionally a few fresh leaves were eaten daily, often in a sandwich to mask their bitterness, to prevent migraines. It was also used to reduce fevers, ease menstrual cramps and inflammatory aches like arthritis, and as a bitter digestive. Modern research supports a modest preventive effect for some migraine sufferers.
whereToFind: Native to southeastern Europe and the Balkans, it is now naturalised widely on walls, waste ground and garden edges. It self-seeds freely in sunny, well-drained spots. Harvest leaves before and during flowering in summer. Seeds and plants are found at garden centers; dried herb and capsules at herb shops and pharmacies.
uses: Carry a feverfew sachet when travelling for protection against accidents and illness
Plant feverfew around the home's borders to purify the air and guard health
Add to a healing charm bag with lavender for headache relief
Use in 'cooling' spells to calm hot tempers
Press the daisy-like flowers in your grimoire for health workings
Hang dried bunches in the kitchen to repel insects
caution: Avoid during pregnancy (it may stimulate the uterus) and breastfeeding, and do not give to children under 2. Stop at least 2 weeks before surgery. Chewing fresh leaves can cause mouth ulcers, lip and tongue swelling and loss of taste, and handling them can cause skin rashes. People allergic to the daisy family (ragweed, chamomile, yarrow) may react. Stopping suddenly after long use can cause rebound headaches, fatigue and joint pain, so taper off. Consult a healthcare provider.
interactions: Increases bleeding risk with blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs such as warfarin, clopidogrel, aspirin and other NSAIDs.
pets: Feverfew is a chrysanthemum relative; the ASPCA lists chrysanthemums as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea, drooling, skin irritation).

name: Horehound
description: A woolly, grey-green mint-family plant with wrinkled leaves and whorls of small white flowers, intensely bitter to the taste. The Egyptians called it 'Seed of Horus' and 'Eye of the Star' and dedicated it to the falcon god. Medieval herbalists considered it a protection against magic and the bite of mad dogs. Its candies and syrups remained a household cough cure well into the twentieth century.
metaphysicalUses: Horehound is a protective herb, carried or hung against sorcery and malicious spirits, and used in exorcism and cleansing incenses. Cunningham notes that it brings mental clarity and quick thinking, and increases creativity. Carry it or drink a little horehound tea before work that needs a sharp mind. It is sacred to Horus and suits rites of the Egyptian pantheon, and was used to balance personal energies. Burn it with frankincense in a protective blend, or scatter it to keep the house free of spiteful influences.
medicalUses: Horehound is one of the oldest cough remedies in Western herbalism. Its bitter syrup, tea or old-fashioned candy was taken for coughs, bronchitis, colds and hoarseness, because it helps loosen mucus. As a bitter, it was also used to stimulate appetite and digestion. The Romans used it as an antidote to poisons, and it was once used for fevers.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean, North Africa and western Asia, it is naturalised in dry pastures, waste places, roadsides and arid hillsides worldwide. It is drought-tolerant and grows easily in poor, sunny soil. Harvest leafy tops as flowering begins in summer. Dried herb, candy drops and syrups are sold by herb suppliers and old-fashioned sweet shops.
uses: Carry a sprig of horehound for protection against malicious magic
Burn horehound and frankincense to exorcise heavy, spiteful energies
Sip a little sweetened horehound tea before study or creative work for clarity
Make horehound and honey syrup for coughs and sore throats (never give honey to babies under 1 year)
Offer horehound on an altar to Horus
Hang a bundle by the door to deter unwelcome spirits
caution: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as it may stimulate the uterus. Large amounts may cause irregular heartbeat and lower blood sugar; use caution with heart conditions or diabetes. Can act as a laxative in high doses. Never give honey (including honey syrups) to babies under 1 year old. Consult a healthcare provider before medicinal use.
interactions: May add to the effects of diabetes medicines and blood pressure medicines. Its tannins may reduce absorption of other drugs, so take medicines at least 30 minutes apart.

name: Licorice Root
description: A leguminous Mediterranean shrub whose sweet, golden root is about fifty times sweeter than sugar. A large cache of licorice root was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. Scythian warriors were said to march for days on it without water. In hoodoo it is a classic root of command and control, while in folk magic it stirs love and lasting sweetness.
metaphysicalUses: Licorice root is used in love and lust spells, and to keep a lover faithful. Chewing a stick of licorice (if safe for you) or carrying it was said to make one passionate. In hoodoo and rootwork, licorice root powder is a classic ingredient in commanding and controlling formulas. It is added to Commanding, Compelling and Controlling oils and powders so the worker's will prevails and others follow their lead. It is used in 'sweetening' work to soften a person's attitude, and in fidelity charms. Bundle it with a written name to bind a lover's attentions to you.
medicalUses: Licorice has a long history as a soothing, demulcent herb for sore throats, coughs, bronchitis and hoarseness, and as a remedy for heartburn, stomach ulcers and digestive inflammation. Traditional Chinese medicine uses it as a 'harmoniser' in many formulas. It was also used to support the adrenals during exhaustion. Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) is used today for the stomach.
whereToFind: Native to southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia, it grows in deep, moist, fertile soils along river valleys. It can be grown in sunny gardens, and roots are harvested after 3-4 years in autumn. Dried root sticks, cut root and powder are sold at herb shops, health food stores, Middle Eastern grocers and hoodoo supply shops.
uses: Add licorice root powder to a commanding oil to assert your will
Carry a stick of licorice root in a red bag to keep a lover faithful
Use in sweetening jars to soften someone's attitude toward you
Sip licorice and marshmallow tea for a raw throat
Write your intention on paper and wrap it around a licorice stick in control work
Include in lust sachets with damiana and cinnamon
caution: Regular or large amounts of whole licorice (glycyrrhizin) can raise blood pressure, lower potassium, cause fluid retention and, in serious cases, irregular heartbeat or cardiac arrest. Avoid with high blood pressure, heart or kidney disease, low potassium or a high-salt diet, and avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Do not use whole licorice for more than 4 to 6 weeks without professional guidance; deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) carries much less of this risk.
interactions: Interacts with diuretics, corticosteroids, digoxin, blood pressure medicines (including ACE inhibitors), stimulant laxatives and other drugs that lower potassium. May also reduce the effect of warfarin and interact with hormonal contraceptives.

name: Marshmallow Root
description: A tall, velvety plant of salt marshes with soft pale-pink flowers. Its root is so full of mucilage that it turns water into a silky gel. The original marshmallow sweet was made from this root's sap whipped with sugar and egg. The genus name comes from the Greek 'althaino', to heal. Since ancient times it has been one of the gentlest healers of the herbal world.
metaphysicalUses: Marshmallow is an herb of protection and of the spirits. Cunningham records that it is burned or carried for protection and to induce psychic powers. Placed on the altar, it draws good spirits. It was traditionally planted on graves, and its root is used in ancestor work to invite benevolent spirits and to soften grief. Because of its soothing nature it is also used in spells to calm and sweeten people, to heal emotional wounds, and to attract gentle love.
medicalUses: Marshmallow root is a premier demulcent in folk herbalism. A cold-water infusion of the root makes a soothing mucilage for sore throats, dry coughs, heartburn, stomach irritation and irritated urinary passages. Poultices of the root and leaves were applied to burns, boils, bruises, splinters and inflamed skin to soften and draw.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, it grows wild in salt marshes, damp meadows, ditches and riverbanks. It grows easily in moist, rich soil in full sun. Dig roots of plants at least two years old in autumn. Dried cut root and powder are sold at herb suppliers and apothecaries; seeds at specialist nurseries.
uses: Place marshmallow root on the altar to invite benevolent spirits
Lay marshmallow root on a loved one's grave to comfort the departed
Carry marshmallow root to strengthen psychic awareness
Make a cold-water infusion of the root to soothe a sore throat
Add to sweetening jars to soften a difficult person
Apply a marshmallow poultice to minor burns or inflamed skin
caution: Generally very safe. It may lower blood sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor levels, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Consult a healthcare provider during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
interactions: Its mucilage may slow absorption of medicines taken at the same time; take medicines at least 1 to 2 hours apart. May add to the effects of diabetes medicines.

name: Slippery Elm
description: A North American elm whose fragrant inner bark becomes slick and slippery when moistened. Native peoples and frontier settlers relied on it as food, wound dressing and medicine, and during the American Revolution soldiers lived on slippery elm gruel. In folk magic, it is famed for its power to stop gossip and slander in its tracks.
metaphysicalUses: Slippery elm is the classic herb for halting gossip. Cunningham records that burning it binds the tongues of those who speak ill of you. Tie a knotted yellow thread around a twist of slippery elm bark and burn it, or keep it in a jar with the gossiper's name to stop slander. In hoodoo it is used to make troubles and enemies 'slide' away. Carrying it in childhood was said to make one persuasive in adulthood. It is also used in court and legal work, to quiet false witnesses and to let the truth slide out.
medicalUses: The powdered inner bark makes a nourishing, soothing gruel or tea that coats and calms the digestive tract and throat. It was used for sore throats, coughs, heartburn, ulcers, diarrhoea and convalescence, when people needed easily digested food. Poultices were applied to wounds, burns, boils and inflammations to soothe and draw out infection.
whereToFind: Native to eastern and central North America, growing in moist woods, river valleys and on rich slopes. Wild populations have been hurt by Dutch elm disease and over-harvesting of bark, so buy only sustainably sourced or cultivated bark, or substitute marshmallow root. Powdered bark and lozenges are sold at herb shops, pharmacies and health food stores.
uses: Burn slippery elm bark to stop gossip and slander against you
Knot a yellow thread around a twist of bark to bind a gossip's tongue
Keep slippery elm with a written name in a jar to silence slander
Carry it to court so lies slide away and truth comes forward
Stir powdered bark into warm water and honey for a soothing gruel
Dissolve a slippery elm lozenge for a raw throat
caution: Generally safe as food-like gruel or lozenges. Serious allergic reactions are possible; stop if you get hives, swelling or trouble breathing. Folk lore claimed the whole bark could cause miscarriage, so avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding unless approved by a healthcare provider. Never give honey (including honey syrups) to babies under 1 year old. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma. Choose sustainable sources, because wild trees are under pressure.
interactions: Its mucilage may slow absorption of medicines; take medicines 1 to 2 hours apart.

name: Black Cohosh
description: A tall woodland plant of eastern North America whose white flower spires glow like 'fairy candles' in summer shade. They carry a strange odour that repels insects, hence 'bugbane'. Its seed pods rattle in autumn wind. Native nations used its dark, knotted root for women's complaints and snakebite, and it later became a staple of nineteenth-century patent medicines.
metaphysicalUses: Black cohosh is a root of courage, protection and potency. It is carried or added to baths to strengthen one's resolve and to banish fear and negative influence. In folk and hoodoo practice it is used in love and potency spells and to strengthen sexual vitality. Sprinkling a tea of the root around a room is said to drive away evil and protect the home. As a dark, earthy root of the deep woods, it is also used in shadow work, rites of the crone and menopause, and rituals that honour the passages of a woman's life.
medicalUses: Native American and Eclectic physicians used black cohosh for menstrual pain, menopausal symptoms, rheumatic and muscular aches, and as an aid in childbirth under skilled care. Today it is best known as a remedy for hot flushes, night sweats and mood changes in menopause, usually as standardised extracts.
whereToFind: Native to rich, moist deciduous woodlands of eastern North America. It is at risk from wild over-harvesting, so grow it yourself in shady woodland gardens or buy cultivated root. Roots are dug in autumn after the fruit ripens. Dried root, tinctures and capsules are sold at herb shops and pharmacies.
uses: Carry a piece of black cohosh root to strengthen courage
Add a root infusion to a ritual bath before facing a difficult confrontation
Sprinkle a cooled infusion around the home to drive away evil
Include in potency and love mojo bags
Place on an altar during croning or menopause rites
Grow it in a shady garden as a protective 'fairy candle' guardian
caution: Avoid during pregnancy (except under skilled supervision at term) and breastfeeding. Rare cases of serious liver injury have been reported; avoid with liver disease and stop and see a provider if you notice dark urine, yellowing skin or eyes, fatigue or abdominal pain. Its safety with hormone-sensitive conditions such as breast or uterine cancer is uncertain, so avoid unless your provider approves. Can cause headache and stomach upset. Do not confuse with blue cohosh, which is more dangerous.
interactions: Use caution with drugs that can harm the liver (such as statins and acetaminophen in high doses), tamoxifen and hormone therapies. Check with a provider if you take any medicines.

name: Goldenseal
description: A small woodland plant of eastern North America with a single white flower and a raspberry-like red fruit. Its gnarled rhizome is bright golden-yellow inside. The Cherokee and Iroquois used it as a dye, wash and medicine. By the late 1800s it was so heavily dug for patent medicines that it became endangered, a sad reminder of greed's toll.
metaphysicalUses: Goldenseal is a solar herb of money and healing. Its golden root is used in money and prosperity spells, sprinkled in business mojo bags, and in rituals for financial success. It is also a powerful healing herb: added to healing incenses and charms and placed beside a candle in healing rituals. Hoodoo practitioners sometimes use it in money-drawing and uncrossing formulas because of its purifying bitterness and gold colour. Because the plant is at risk, many practitioners now use only a small pinch or a picture of the root, which shows respect for the plant spirit.
medicalUses: Goldenseal was used by Native American healers and later Eclectic physicians as a bitter, antiseptic herb for mucous membranes. Folk use included washes for sore eyes and skin infections, gargles for mouth and throat infections, and remedies for digestive inflammation and catarrhal colds. It was applied to wounds to prevent infection.
whereToFind: Native to rich, shady hardwood forests of eastern North America. It is listed as at-risk (CITES Appendix II), so never harvest wild plants. Grow it in a shady woodland garden or buy only certified cultivated root. Oregon grape root is a sustainable alternative. Dried cultivated root, powder and tinctures are sold at herb shops.
uses: Add a pinch of cultivated goldenseal to a money mojo bag
Sprinkle a little powder around a green candle for business success
Place beside a blue candle in healing rituals
Use as a gargle for sore throat, under guidance
Grow it in a shade garden as a living prosperity charm and an act of conservation
Substitute Oregon grape root in spells to protect the wild plant
caution: Short-term use only; safety beyond a few weeks is unknown. Do not use during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and never give it to infants, because its berberine can harm newborns (it can worsen jaundice). Avoid with high blood pressure. Use only cultivated sources, since the plant is threatened, and buy tested products because adulteration is common. Consult a healthcare provider before use.
interactions: Strongly inhibits liver enzymes (CYP3A4 and CYP2D6), so it can raise levels of many drugs, including some statins, blood pressure drugs, immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine, and antidepressants. It lowered metformin levels by about 25 percent in a study, which could weaken blood sugar control.

name: Ginseng
description: A slow-growing understory plant whose forked root can grow strikingly human in shape. This gave it the Chinese name 'ren shen', 'man root', and made it one of the most prized roots in Asian medicine for over two thousand years. American ginseng was 'sang' to Appalachian diggers who sold it for silver. A wild root many decades old may be worth a fortune.
metaphysicalUses: Ginseng is a root of vitality, longevity, love and wishes. Carry the root to attract love and to guard health, beauty and sexual potency. Cunningham records a wish spell: hold a ginseng root, visualise your wish carved on it, then toss it into running water. Because of its human shape it is sometimes used as a safer substitute for mandrake in poppet and image magic. It is used in rituals to gain energy and endurance, and burned or carried to ward off evil.
medicalUses: In traditional Chinese and Korean medicine, ginseng is a supreme tonic for the qi. It is used to restore energy after illness, combat fatigue and stress, sharpen focus and support immune function and longevity. Native Americans and Appalachian folk healers used American ginseng, a cooler and gentler root, as a tonic and to ease nausea and exhaustion. Modern herbalists class it as an adaptogen.
whereToFind: Asian ginseng is native to the cool mountain forests of Korea, northeast China and Russia's Far East. American ginseng grows in rich, shady hardwood forests of eastern North America. Wild ginseng is endangered and protected by law, so harvesting is regulated or banned. Buy cultivated or 'woods-grown' root. Dried root, slices and teas are found at Asian groceries, herb shops and health food stores.
uses: Carry a ginseng root in a red bag for love, vitality and potency
Whisper a wish into a ginseng root and cast it into a river
Use a forked ginseng root as a poppet in place of mandrake
Simmer a few slices in tea during long, draining days
Add to longevity and health charms
Burn a little powdered root to ward off evil
caution: May cause insomnia, headaches, nervousness and changes in blood pressure. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, in children, and with hormone-sensitive conditions. It may lower blood sugar, so monitor levels with diabetes, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Do not use long-term without breaks. Buy only cultivated root, since wild ginseng is protected. Consult a healthcare provider. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
interactions: May reduce the effect of warfarin (American ginseng) or increase bleeding with other blood thinners, and may add to diabetes medicines (low blood sugar). Avoid with MAOIs (such as phenelzine), stimulants and caffeine, and use caution with antidepressants and immunosuppressants.

name: High John the Conqueror
partsUsed: root (tuber), whole or chips, used for carrying only
description: The dark, knobbly root of a Mexican morning glory, and the most famous root of African American hoodoo. It is named for High John, a legendary enslaved trickster-prince whose wit and laughter could never be broken by his masters. Zora Neale Hurston wrote that his power was hidden in the root so that his people might always have hope. It is the king of roots for luck, mastery, money and manly power.
metaphysicalUses: High John the Conqueror is carried for mastery, personal power, luck, success and sexual prowess. A whole root is dressed with High John or Van Van oil and placed in a red flannel mojo bag, often with a silver dime, to bring luck in gambling, money, love and all endeavours. Rootworkers say it helps you conquer any situation, overcome obstacles and enemies, and command respect. It is also used in uncrossing and to restore confidence and strength to anyone who feels beaten down. Root chips are added to candle dressings, and the root is soaked in whiskey or oil to make High John oil. Feed the root regularly with oil or whiskey to keep it strong.
medicalUses: Historically jalap root was used in Western medicine as a powerful purgative laxative. It is a harsh, drastic purgative that is no longer considered safe for home use. In hoodoo the root is carried and anointed, never eaten.
whereToFind: The plant is native to Mexico, especially the mountains around Xalapa (Jalapa) in Veracruz, which gave jalap its name. Whole roots, chips and High John oil are sold at hoodoo and spiritual supply shops, botanicas and occult stores. Beware of fakes and substitutions, and buy from reputable rootworkers.
uses: Carry a whole root in a red flannel bag with a silver dime for luck and success
Anoint the root weekly with High John oil or whiskey to keep it fed and powerful
Steep root chips in oil to make High John the Conqueror oil for candles
Hold the root while you pray or state your intention before a job interview
Place a root under a gold candle for victory over obstacles
Keep a root in the cash register for business success
Read Zora Neale Hurston's 'High John de Conquer' to honour the tradition
caution: POISONOUS: jalap root is a violent purgative and can cause severe cramps, vomiting, diarrhea and dehydration if eaten. Never ingest it, and do not put High John oil on broken skin or mucous membranes. Keep roots and oils away from children and pets. Wash hands after handling.
pets: Keep roots and oils away from pets; chewing the root can cause severe vomiting and diarrhea.

name: Cinquefoil
description: A creeping, strawberry-like plant with bright yellow flowers and leaves divided into five leaflets, like a little open hand. Medieval knights painted it on their shields as a sign of self-mastery. It was said to be a key ingredient in witches' flying ointments. In hoodoo, as 'five-finger grass', it is the herb that can do anything five fingers can do.
metaphysicalUses: Cinquefoil is a versatile herb of luck, money, protection and influence. The five points of the leaf stand for love, money, health, power and wisdom, so carrying it grants all five. In hoodoo, five-finger grass is used so that 'whatever five fingers can do, it can undo'. It protects against harm, draws money, removes curses and helps you win favours. An old custom says that a cinquefoil leaf with seven points, placed under the pillow, will bring a dream of your future love. Carry it to court so justice will be granted and to speak eloquently. Hang it at the door or over the bed for protection, and wash your hands and forehead nine times in a cinquefoil infusion to wash away hexes.
medicalUses: Cinquefoil is a gentle astringent in folk herbalism. Tea and gargles were used for diarrhoea, sore throats, mouth ulcers and loose gums, and it was given for fevers. Washes and compresses were applied to inflamed skin and minor wounds. Culpeper recommended it for fevers and inflammations.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia and naturalised elsewhere, creeping cinquefoil spreads along hedgerows, grassy verges, pastures and lawns, flowering through summer. It grows easily in sun or light shade. Gather leaves in summer. Dried five-finger grass is sold by hoodoo supply shops, botanicas and herb suppliers.
uses: Carry five-finger grass in a mojo bag for love, money, health, power and wisdom
Hang a bundle over the door to protect the home
Wash hands and forehead nine times in a cinquefoil infusion to wash away hexes
Place a seven-pointed leaf under your pillow to dream of your future love
Carry it to court to speak eloquently and win favours
Add to money-drawing powders with cinnamon
Gargle a cooled infusion for a sore throat
caution: Generally safe in moderate, short-term amounts. Its tannins can upset sensitive stomachs, and long-term high doses are not advised. Avoid medicinal use during pregnancy and breastfeeding unless approved by a healthcare provider.
interactions: Tannins may reduce absorption of other medicines and iron; take them a couple of hours apart.

name: Devil's Shoestring
latin: Viburnum alnifolium (also Viburnum opulus; historically Tephrosia virginiana)
description: The long, wiry, tangling roots of several plants, most often hobblebush viburnum, whose low branches root where they touch the earth and trip unwary walkers. That is why it is also called 'witch hobble'. In hoodoo these 'shoestrings' are used to trip up the Devil and any enemies who mean you harm, and to tie down good fortune.
metaphysicalUses: Devil's shoestring is a hoodoo root of protection, luck and binding. Pieces are carried in the pocket or laid across doorways to 'trip up' the Devil and keep evil, enemies and harm from reaching you. Gamblers soak short lengths in whiskey or camphor and carry them for luck. Job seekers carry it to 'tie down' a job or promotion. It is used in binding work to hobble an enemy and to control situations, and nine pieces are sometimes tied together in a protective charm. Some workers chew a little root before asking for a raise. This is not recommended, since it should not be eaten; simply carry it instead.
medicalUses: The related cramp bark (Viburnum opulus) is used in Western herbalism as a muscle relaxant for menstrual cramps and muscle spasms. However, the roots sold as 'devil's shoestring' may come from several plants, so they should be used only for magic, never internally.
whereToFind: Hobblebush is native to the moist, shady forests of eastern North America and the Appalachians. Commercial devil's shoestring is sold as dried root pieces at hoodoo and spiritual supply shops, botanicas and occult stores. Identity can vary between sellers.
uses: Carry a short length of devil's shoestring in the pocket to trip up evil
Lay nine pieces across a doorway or under the doormat for protection
Soak in whiskey and carry in a gambling mojo for luck (never drink the soaking whiskey)
Carry to a job interview to 'tie down' the job
Bind an enemy's name with a shoestring to hobble their harmful plans
Nail a piece over the threshold to keep the Devil out
caution: For magical, non-ingestive use only. Commercial roots may come from several different plants, some of which (such as Tephrosia virginiana) contain rotenone and other toxic compounds. Do not eat, chew or brew them, and do not soak them in drinks you will consume. Wash hands after handling, and keep away from children and pets.
pets: Keep roots away from pets; some source plants contain rotenone, which is toxic to animals.

name: Solomon's Seal
description: A graceful woodland plant whose arching stems hang with creamy bell-like flowers, later dark blue-black berries. When a stem falls away in autumn, it leaves a round scar on the rhizome resembling a seal. Legend says King Solomon himself set his seal upon the root to mark its virtues. As the 'seal' of the wise king, it has long been used to seal spells and bind vows.
metaphysicalUses: Solomon's seal is an herb of protection, binding and sacred seals. Cunningham advises placing the root in the four corners of the house for protection and adding an infusion of it to exorcism and offertory incense. In ceremonial and hoodoo practice it is used to 'seal' a spell, an oath, a promise or a pact, binding the work so it holds fast. It is associated with the wisdom of King Solomon and is used in rituals for wisdom and spiritual authority, in spirit conjuration and in consecrating sacred space. Hoodoo practitioners carry it for wisdom, protection and success.
medicalUses: European folk medicine applied poultices of the bruised root to bruises, black eyes and freckles, and salves to sprains and minor wounds. It was also used for joint and tendon complaints. In Chinese medicine, related species (Huang Jing) are used as a nourishing tonic, but European Solomon's seal can cause nausea when eaten, and the berries are toxic.
whereToFind: Native to temperate woodlands of Europe, Asia and North America, growing in shady deciduous forests, hedgerows and woodland edges. It is easy to grow in a shady garden in moist, humus-rich soil. Dig rhizomes in autumn from your own plantings, leaving plenty to regrow. Dried root is sold by herb suppliers and hoodoo shops.
uses: Place a piece of Solomon's seal root in each corner of the house for protection
Burn powdered root with frankincense to seal and bind a completed spell
Keep it beside a written oath or contract to bind the agreement
Add to offertory and exorcism incense
Carry it for wisdom before making important decisions
Plant it in a shade garden as a guardian of sacred space
caution: The berries are poisonous and can cause vomiting and diarrhea; keep them away from children and pets. All parts of European species can cause nausea if eaten. Do not take internally; use externally or for magic unless guided by a qualified herbalist, and avoid it entirely during pregnancy and breastfeeding and with diabetes. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
interactions: If taken internally, it may lower blood sugar and add to the effects of diabetes medicines.
pets: All parts, especially the berries, are harmful to dogs and cats if eaten (vomiting, diarrhea).

name: Agrimony
description: A tall, softly hairy herb of hedgerows whose slender spikes of small yellow flowers rise like church steeples, later becoming burrs that cling to passing clothes. Anglo-Saxons prized it as a wound-healer, and the 'eau d'arquebusade' of French soldiers treated gunshot wounds with it. In folk magic it is one of the foremost herbs for returning hexes to their sender.
metaphysicalUses: Agrimony is a powerful protective and counter-magic herb. Cunningham notes that it is used in protection sachets and spells, and that it banishes negative energies and spirits and reverses spells, sending hexes back to the sender. Placed under the head, it was said to cause a deep sleep that lasts until it is removed, as in the old English verse 'If it be leyd under mann's heed, He shal sleepyn as he were deed'. Use it in uncrossing baths, protective sachets and mirror-box spells that return harm. It is also used to give courage, and to clear psychic blocks and inner turmoil.
medicalUses: In traditional European herbalism, agrimony was a gentle astringent tonic. Tea and gargles were used for sore throats, hoarseness, diarrhoea, mild digestive complaints and liver sluggishness. Washes and poultices were applied to wounds, cuts and skin sores to stop bleeding and promote healing. Herbalists also gave it for urinary weakness.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia, it grows along hedgerows, roadsides, field margins and dry grassy banks, flowering in summer. It grows easily from seed in sunny, well-drained soil. Harvest the flowering tops in summer. Dried herb is sold at herb suppliers and apothecaries.
uses: Add agrimony to a mirror box spell to return a hex to its sender
Tuck into a protective sachet with rue and salt
Place under the pillow for deep, untroubled sleep (remove it in the morning)
Bathe in an agrimony infusion for uncrossing
Burn as incense to banish negative spirits from a room
Gargle a cooled agrimony infusion for a sore throat
caution: Generally safe in moderate, short-term amounts. Its tannins may cause constipation or stomach upset. Not recommended for children under 12, or during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Consult a healthcare provider if you take blood thinners or diabetes medication. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
interactions: May affect blood clotting and blood sugar, so use caution with anticoagulants and diabetes medicines. Tannins may reduce absorption of other drugs and iron; take them a couple of hours apart.

name: Wood Betony
description: A pretty mint-family plant of woods and meadows with dense spikes of magenta flowers. It was so esteemed in the ancient and medieval world that Antonius Musa, physician to Emperor Augustus, wrote it could cure 47 ailments. An Italian proverb advised selling one's coat to buy betony. It was planted in churchyards and worn as an amulet against evil spirits and nightmares.
metaphysicalUses: Wood betony is a classic herb of protection, purification and dreams. Burned at midsummer, it purifies and protects. Placed under the pillow, it prevents nightmares and brings prophetic dreams. Planted or hung around the home, it guards against evil, and scattered across doorways it forms a barrier no evil can cross. Cunningham notes it can be added to love incense and sachets, and carried to strengthen body and mind. Many old traditions use it in exorcism and to lift despair and dispel melancholy.
medicalUses: Betony was a cornerstone of medieval herbal medicine. Folk healers used it for headaches, nervous tension, anxiety and melancholy, as a gentle digestive tonic, and to heal wounds and ulcers. Culpeper wrote that it was 'a very precious herb' that was 'good for the head'. Modern herbalists still use it as a gentle nervine for tension headaches.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, it grows in open woods, hedgebanks, heaths and grassy meadows, flowering in summer. It is easy to grow in a sunny or partly shaded garden. Harvest the flowering tops in summer. Dried herb is sold at herb suppliers; plants at specialist nurseries. (American 'wood betony', Pedicularis, is a different plant.)
uses: Scatter dried betony across the threshold as a barrier against evil
Burn betony on Midsummer Eve to purify and protect
Place a sprig under the pillow to prevent nightmares
Wear a betony amulet to lift melancholy
Brew a gentle tea for a tension headache
Plant betony around the home for protection
caution: Generally safe in moderate amounts. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as it was traditionally considered a uterine stimulant. Large doses may cause stomach upset. People taking blood pressure medication should consult a healthcare provider. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
interactions: May add to the effects of blood pressure medicines.

name: Meadowsweet
description: A tall plant of damp meadows and riverbanks with frothy cream flower heads that smell of almond and honey. It was used to flavour mead, which gave it the name 'meadwort', and strewn at weddings, hence 'bridewort'. In Welsh myth the magicians Math and Gwydion made the flower-maiden Blodeuwedd from oak, broom and meadowsweet. Druids held it as one of their three most sacred herbs, along with vervain and water mint. Salicylic acid was first isolated from its buds, and the name 'aspirin' comes from its old botanical name, Spiraea.
metaphysicalUses: Meadowsweet is a flower of love, peace and joy. Fresh flowers placed on the altar during love spells, or added to love mixtures, bring a gentle, faithful love. Strewn in the house, it keeps peace. Worn at Lammas, it helps you see the faery folk and brings joy. It is a traditional bridal herb, woven into handfasting garlands and bouquets. Old lore says that if you are robbed, placing meadowsweet on water will reveal the thief: if it sinks, the thief is a man; if it floats, a woman. It is sacred to Blodeuwedd and suits rituals of the flower maiden and Beltane.
medicalUses: Meadowsweet is a beloved folk remedy for the stomach. Herbalists used it to settle acid indigestion, heartburn and stomach upset, and to ease fevers, headaches and the aches of rheumatism and arthritis, thanks to its natural salicylates. Unlike aspirin, it was considered gentle on the stomach.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and western Asia and naturalised in parts of North America, it grows in wet meadows, along ditches, streams, riverbanks and marshes, flowering from early to late summer. Easy to grow in moist, rich soil in sun or part shade. Gather flowers on a dry day when freshly open. Dried herb is sold at herb suppliers and apothecaries.
uses: Weave meadowsweet into a handfasting garland or bridal bouquet
Strew dried flowers through the house to keep the peace
Place fresh flowers on the altar during love spells
Wear a sprig at Lammas to glimpse the faery folk
Brew a gentle tea for heartburn and acid indigestion
Honour Blodeuwedd at Beltane with a crown of meadowsweet, broom and oak
caution: Contains salicylates (aspirin-like compounds): avoid if you are allergic or sensitive to aspirin, have aspirin-triggered asthma, a bleeding disorder or stomach ulcers. Do not give to children or teenagers, especially with fever or a viral illness, because of the risk of Reye's syndrome. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Consult a healthcare provider.
interactions: May increase bleeding with blood thinners (warfarin, clopidogrel) and add to the effects of aspirin, other NSAIDs and bismuth subsalicylate.
pets: Salicylates are especially dangerous to cats; do not give meadowsweet preparations to pets.

name: Vetiver
description: A tall clumping grass of India whose fragrant roots go straight down several metres, binding soil against erosion. Its oil smells deep, smoky and earthy, like damp roots and rain, and in India is called 'the oil of tranquility'. Mats of woven khus root are hung in doorways and sprinkled with water to cool and perfume homes in the summer heat. In hoodoo and Caribbean folk magic it is a root of money, luck and love.
metaphysicalUses: Vetiver is a deeply grounding root of money, luck and love. Cunningham notes it is added to love sachets and bath water to make a person more attractive, and burned in incense to overcome hexes. Placed in the cash register, it draws money. Carried, it brings luck. It is a key ingredient in many hoodoo and Caribbean formulas, such as Van Van and Money Drawing oils, and in New Orleans voodoo it is used for luck and protection. Its deep roots make it ideal for grounding after ritual or psychic work, for stability in business and home, and for breaking hexes.
medicalUses: In Ayurveda, vetiver (khus) is a cooling herb. Its root water and sherbet are used to soothe heat, thirst and fever, and its oil is used to calm the mind and ease stress, anxiety and insomnia. In aromatherapy, diluted vetiver oil is used for nervous exhaustion and grounding, and in skincare for oily and irritated skin.
whereToFind: Native to India and widely cultivated in tropical regions such as Haiti, Indonesia and Java, often planted for erosion control. It can be grown in warm climates in sunny, moist soil, or in large pots. Dried roots, essential oil and khus mats are sold by herb suppliers, Indian groceries, aromatherapy stores and hoodoo shops.
uses: Keep a bundle of vetiver root in the cash register to draw money
Add vetiver to love bath sachets to increase attraction
Burn vetiver in incense to break hexes
Diffuse vetiver oil after ritual for grounding
Carry a sachet of vetiver root for luck
Hang a khus mat in a sunny window and mist it to cool and bless the home
Add a few drops of oil to a money candle dressing
caution: Generally safe. Dilute the essential oil (about 1 to 3 percent in a carrier oil) before applying to skin, and patch test. Avoid the essential oil during pregnancy without professional guidance. Do not ingest essential oil. Diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room. Burn only small amounts in a fireproof dish in a ventilated room, never leave it unattended, and keep smoke away from children, pets and people with asthma.
pets: Essential oils are dangerous to cats; do not diffuse or apply them where cats live or groom.

name: Lemongrass
description: A tall, tropical grass with long blades and a bright, lemony fragrance. It is essential to Thai, Vietnamese and Caribbean cooking. In Jamaica it is 'fever grass', brewed for colds and fevers. In hoodoo it is the soul of Van Van oil, the famous New Orleans formula for clearing away evil and opening the road to luck.
metaphysicalUses: Lemongrass is a powerful cleansing and road-opening herb. It is the key ingredient in Van Van oil, a New Orleans classic used to clear away evil, cross conditions and bad luck, and to open the way for success. Cunningham notes that lemongrass planted around the home repels snakes, and that it is used in lust potions and to develop psychic powers. Floor washes made of lemongrass cleanse the home and business of negativity. It is also used to clear the mind before divination, and to bring fresh starts and good fortune.
medicalUses: In Caribbean, Brazilian and Southeast Asian folk medicine, lemongrass tea (fever grass) is a favourite remedy for fevers, colds and flu, indigestion, bloating and nervous tension. Diluted essential oil is used in aromatherapy for muscle pain and as an insect repellent, and it is a common ingredient in natural deodorants and soaps.
whereToFind: Native to tropical Asia and widely grown in the tropics. It can be grown in pots and brought indoors in cooler climates, in full sun with rich, moist soil. Root a stalk bought from the grocery in water and plant it. Fresh stalks are sold at Asian groceries and supermarkets; dried herb and essential oil at herb shops and aromatherapy suppliers.
uses: Make Van Van oil with lemongrass to clear away evil and open the road
Mop floors with a lemongrass wash to cleanse the home and business
Brew lemongrass tea before divination to clear the mind
Plant lemongrass around the home for protection
Add a few drops of diluted oil to a spray to repel insects
Use in road-opening candle dressings
Simmer lemongrass stalks on the stove to refresh a stagnant home
caution: Safe in food amounts. Avoid medicinal doses and the essential oil during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The essential oil can irritate and sensitize the skin, so dilute it to about 1 percent or less and patch test, and keep it away from eyes and children's faces. Never ingest essential oil.
pets: The ASPCA lists lemongrass as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (stomach upset in pets; breathing problems in horses). Essential oils are dangerous to cats; do not diffuse or apply them where cats live or groom.

name: Mandrake
partsUsed: root (kept whole, for symbolic and talismanic use only)
description: A low Mediterranean plant with a rosette of broad leaves, bell-shaped violet or greenish flowers and golden, sweet-smelling fruits. Its thick, forked root often looks uncannily like a human body. Legend says that the root shrieked when pulled from the ground, killing anyone who heard it, so it was tied to a hungry dog that dragged it out. It was said to grow beneath the gallows from the spilled seed of hanged men. It is the most legendary of all magical plants.
metaphysicalUses: Mandrake root is the archetypal plant ally of the witch. A whole root is kept in the home on the mantel, for protection, prosperity and fertility. Cunningham notes that it guards the home and averts misfortune. Carried, it is said to attract love. The root, when activated, was traditionally 'awakened' by leaving it undisturbed for three days and then placing it in warm water overnight. It may be used as a poppet or image of a person in sympathetic magic, or kept as a familiar or house spirit called the Alraun, which was dressed, fed and cared for. Money placed beside it was said to multiply. Many modern practitioners use a carved root, a drawing, or ginseng, bryony or apple root as a safer substitute.
medicalUses: Historically, mandrake was used in ancient and medieval medicine as an anaesthetic and sleeping draught before surgery, and as a painkiller. These uses were dangerous and frequently fatal, and have no place in modern home practice.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean region and the Middle East, it grows in dry, sunny, stony soil, fields and olive groves. It can be grown by experienced gardeners in a deep pot or well-drained bed, away from children and pets. Whole dried roots are sometimes sold by occult shops and specialist herb suppliers. Be careful: 'American mandrake' (mayapple, Podophyllum) and 'English mandrake' (white bryony) are different, but equally poisonous.
uses: Keep a whole dried mandrake root on the mantel for protection and prosperity
Lay a silver coin beside the root to multiply money
Care for the root as a house spirit, wrapped in silk or linen
Use a carved ginseng or apple root as a safer mandrake substitute in poppet magic
Draw or paint a mandrake in your grimoire as a protective emblem
Grow it in a locked or out-of-reach pot as a living talisman
caution: POISONOUS: all parts of mandrake contain tropane alkaloids (atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine) and can cause hallucinations, delirium, rapid heartbeat, coma and death. Never eat, smoke, burn, brew or apply it to skin. Wear gloves when handling and wash your hands afterward. Keep away from children and pets, and store in a sealed, labeled container. Seek emergency help immediately if any is swallowed.
pets: Highly toxic to pets; keep the root and plant completely out of reach.

name: Belladonna
partsUsed: none for use; studied in lore and garden only
description: A tall, shadowy perennial with dull purple bells and glossy black berries as tempting as cherries. Its genus is named for Atropos, the Fate who cuts the thread of life, and 'bella donna', 'beautiful lady', recalls Renaissance women who dropped its juice into their eyes to make their pupils large and dark. It is one of the plants named in old recipes for witches' flying ointments. The Scots are said to have poisoned an invading Danish army with belladonna-laced wine.
metaphysicalUses: Belladonna's power in modern witchcraft is symbolic and in lore. It belongs to Hecate and the Fates, and is a potent emblem of the poison path, of death and rebirth, and of the boundary between worlds. Practitioners honour it in shadow work and ancestor rites, as an image or a sealed, labelled specimen on the altar, never consumed. It was a famous ingredient in historical flying ointments and is linked to astral travel and visionary trance. Today, those experiences are approached safely through meditation and journeying with its image. Its 'beautiful lady' name links it to glamour and dangerous allure. Grow it, draw it or study it with respect.
medicalUses: Its alkaloid atropine is used in modern medicine under strict medical control, for example to dilate pupils and treat certain heart conditions and poisonings. Historically, crude belladonna preparations were used as painkillers and antispasmodics, but home use is extremely dangerous and has caused many deaths.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, it grows in shady woodland, on chalky or limestone soils, around old ruins and in waste ground. It is sometimes grown by poison-garden enthusiasts in secured beds. It should not be grown where children, pets or livestock can reach it. Many regions restrict its sale.
uses: Keep a botanical drawing or photograph of belladonna on a Hecate altar
Meditate on its image during shadow work about death and rebirth
Study it in a public poison garden to learn its lore safely
Draw its bell-shaped flower and berry in your grimoire as an emblem of the poison path
Use mugwort or a guided journey instead of flying ointments for astral work
Wear gloves if you encounter it in the garden, and warn others
caution: POISONOUS: belladonna is one of the most toxic plants in Europe. All parts, especially the berries and roots, contain atropine and scopolamine and can cause dilated pupils, blurred vision, delirium, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, seizures and death. A few berries can seriously poison or kill a child. Never eat, smoke, burn, brew it or apply it to skin or eyes. Wear gloves when handling, keep away from children and pets, and seek emergency help immediately if exposure occurs.
pets: Highly toxic to dogs, cats and livestock.

name: Foxglove
partsUsed: none for use; grown in the garden for protection
description: A tall, stately biennial with towering spires of speckled purple or white bells, beloved by bumblebees and the fair folk. Its name may be 'folk's glove', for the faeries are said to give the flowers to foxes to wear on their paws so they may sneak silently into henhouses. The spots inside the bells are said to be the fingerprints of elves. In 1785, William Withering discovered it was a powerful heart medicine, which gave us digitalis.
metaphysicalUses: Foxglove is a faery plant and a guardian of the home. Growing it in the garden protects the house and grounds and invites the good will of the fair folk. Old Irish and Welsh lore warns against bringing the flowers indoors, as this may offend the faeries, and in some places it was believed the plant could bring back a child stolen by the fair folk. Foxglove is honoured in faery work by planting it, leaving offerings beside it and meditating on it as a doorway to the otherworld. Its bells are a vivid emblem in spells for protection and heart-healing, but only through imagery, never by handling or using the plant itself.
medicalUses: Foxglove is the source of digoxin and digitoxin, life-saving heart medicines used only under strict medical supervision. Historically, folk healers used foxglove for 'dropsy' (heart-failure swelling), but the difference between a healing dose and a lethal one is very small, and home use has killed many people.
whereToFind: Native to western and southern Europe, it grows in woodland clearings, hedgebanks, heaths and rocky hillsides, especially on acidic soils, flowering in early summer. It is a popular cottage-garden plant sold in garden centers and seed catalogues. If you grow it, keep it away from children and pets and wear gloves when deadheading.
uses: Grow foxglove at the edge of the garden to protect the home and welcome the faeries
Leave a small offering of milk or honey beside the plant for the fair folk
Paint or press a single bloom (with gloves) for your grimoire's faery pages
Meditate beside a flowering foxglove to journey to the otherworld
Plant it for bumblebees as a gift to the land spirits
Use its image in a protection sigil or heart-healing charm
caution: POISONOUS: every part of foxglove contains cardiac glycosides that can cause nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, irregular heartbeat and fatal heart failure. Never eat, brew or apply any part. Do not confuse its leaves with comfrey or borage, as this has caused deaths. Wear gloves when handling, and wash hands afterward. Keep away from children and pets. Seek emergency medical help immediately if any part is swallowed.
pets: Highly toxic to dogs, cats and horses (heart rhythm problems, vomiting).

name: Datura
partsUsed: none for use; grown or studied for lore only
description: A rank-smelling annual with huge white or violet trumpet flowers that unfurl at dusk and glow like ghosts under the moon, followed by spiky 'thorn apple' seed pods. Its name 'jimsonweed' comes from Jamestown, Virginia, where in 1676 British soldiers who ate it in a salad went mad for eleven days. In India it is offered to Shiva. In many cultures it is linked to sorcery, prophecy and the spirit world.
metaphysicalUses: Datura's magic today is symbolic, botanical and devotional. Cunningham notes old lore that it breaks hexes and protects when sprinkled around the home, and that a sealed sprig was placed in a shoe or hat against evil. In Hindu tradition its flowers and fruits are offered to Shiva, especially at Maha Shivaratri. As the 'moonflower' that opens at night, it is a striking emblem in moon magic and shadow work.
