Honour it by growing it in a secure spot, sitting with its blooms at dusk or using its image on a Hecate or night altar. Its traditional visionary use is extremely dangerous, so approach those realms only through safe meditation and journeying.
medicalUses: Historically, datura leaves were smoked in 'asthma cigarettes' and used in salves, and its alkaloids appear in some controlled medicines. These folk uses were very dangerous and caused many poisonings; they have no place in home practice.
whereToFind: Probably native to the Americas, it now grows worldwide in disturbed ground, fields, roadsides and waste places, flowering from summer to autumn. Some ornamental Datura species are sold at garden centers. Grow only where children, pets and livestock cannot reach it, and wear gloves when handling.
uses: Grow datura in a secured bed as a living guardian of a night garden
Sit with its moon-white blooms at dusk to meditate on the threshold between worlds
Place a photograph or drawing of the flower on a Shiva or Hecate altar
Sketch the spiked seed pod in your grimoire as a protective hex-breaking emblem
Keep a single dried seed pod sealed in a labelled glass jar as a warding curio, out of reach
Wear gloves and wash your hands after any contact with the plant
caution: POISONOUS: all parts of datura, especially the seeds, contain tropane alkaloids (scopolamine, atropine, hyoscyamine). Even small amounts can cause terrifying delirium, hallucinations, high fever, rapid heartbeat, seizures, coma and death, and potency varies wildly between plants. Never eat, smoke, burn, brew or apply it to skin. Keep it away from children and pets, and seek emergency help immediately if exposure occurs.
pets: Highly toxic to dogs, cats and livestock.

name: Henbane
partsUsed: none for use; studied for lore only
description: A sticky, foul-smelling, hairy plant with pale yellow flowers veined in deep purple, like bloodshot eyes. Its name may mean 'hen killer'. It was burned by Apollo's priestesses, used in Norse and Celtic rites, and brewed into German beer until the Bavarian Purity Law of 1516 banned it. Medieval witches were said to add it to flying ointments, and in Hamlet, the king's 'cursed hebenon' poured into the ear may be henbane.
metaphysicalUses: Henbane belongs to the poison path and the old gods of prophecy and storm. In history it was burned for divination and to summon spirits, and Cunningham records it in love lore: a man who wears it is said to attract a woman. In Germanic folklore, henbane was thrown into water as rain magic, to bring rain in drought. In modern practice, honour henbane only symbolically: through its image on a Saturnian or ancestral altar, through study of its history, or by growing it secured in a poison garden. Work with its themes of death, prophecy and the underworld through meditation, never through smoke or ingestion.
medicalUses: Historically, henbane was used as a sedative, painkiller and anaesthetic, and its alkaloids (hyoscyamine and scopolamine) are still used in controlled pharmaceutical medicines. Crude home preparations are extremely dangerous and have caused many deaths.
whereToFind: Native to Europe and Asia and naturalised in North America, henbane grows in sandy waste ground, roadsides, old farmyards, ruins and coastal areas. It is a declared noxious weed in some places. Seeds are sometimes sold for poison gardens, but it should be grown only by experienced, responsible gardeners in secured spaces.
uses: Place a drawing of henbane's purple-veined flower on an ancestor altar
Study its history in Norse, Greek and medieval lore as part of poison path research
Meditate on its image when working with themes of prophecy and death
Grow it only in a secured, labelled poison garden bed
Use mugwort or guided journeying for spirit and divination work instead
Wear gloves if handling, and wash hands afterward
caution: POISONOUS: all parts of henbane contain tropane alkaloids that can cause delirium, hallucinations, convulsions, respiratory failure and death. Even smoke from burning the plant or seeds is dangerous. Never eat, smoke, burn, brew it or apply it to skin. Keep away from children and pets, and seek emergency help immediately if exposure occurs.
pets: Highly toxic to pets and livestock.

name: Wolfsbane
partsUsed: none for use; grown or studied for lore only
description: A tall, stately plant with deep blue-violet flowers shaped like a monk's hood or helmet, among the most poisonous plants in Europe. Greek myth says it sprang from the slavering foam of Cerberus when Heracles dragged him from the underworld, and Hecate and Medea used it in their potions. Its name comes from its use in baits and arrows to kill wolves. In folk lore it protects against werewolves and vampires.
metaphysicalUses: Wolfsbane is sacred to Hecate and is one of the great plants of the poison path. Cunningham notes that its seed was once wrapped in a lizard skin and carried for invisibility, and that it was used to protect against werewolves and vampires. Today it is honoured purely symbolically: its image on a Hecate altar at the dark moon, its story told at Samhain, or a living plant grown securely in a garden as a protective guardian. It is a potent emblem of protection, transformation and the underworld, and of the power that comes from respecting danger.
medicalUses: Aconite was historically used in tiny doses as a painkiller and fever reducer, and it still appears in highly diluted homoeopathic and some processed traditional Asian preparations. Crude aconite is extremely poisonous; it has caused many deaths and has no place in home herbalism.
whereToFind: Native to the mountains of western and central Europe, growing in damp meadows, mountain woods and along streams. It is sold as an ornamental perennial at garden centers. Gardeners should always wear gloves, as poison can be absorbed through the skin, and plant it away from children, pets and vegetable beds.
uses: Grow monkshood in a secured border as a guardian against evil
Place a drawing of its helmet-shaped flower on a Hecate altar at the dark moon
Tell the myth of Cerberus and wolfsbane at Samhain
Use its image in protective sigils against predatory forces
Study it in a public poison garden to learn its lore safely
Always wear gloves when gardening near it, and wash hands afterward
caution: POISONOUS: wolfsbane is one of the deadliest plants known. All parts, especially the roots, contain aconitine, which can be absorbed through the skin and causes tingling and numbness, vomiting, irregular heartbeat, paralysis and death. Never eat, brew, burn or apply it. Always wear gloves when handling, keep away from children and pets, and seek emergency help immediately if exposure occurs.
pets: Highly toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

name: Pennyroyal
partsUsed: dried leaves, for non-ingestive charms only
description: A low, creeping mint with tiny lilac flowers and a sharp, pungent scent. Its Latin name 'pulegium' comes from 'pulex', flea, because the Romans used it to drive fleas out of the bedding. In Greek myth, Demeter broke her fast with a drink of barley, water and pennyroyal (the kykeon) while searching for Persephone, and it was drunk in the Eleusinian Mysteries. Sailors carried it to purify stale drinking water, but today it is known to be dangerously toxic.
metaphysicalUses: Pennyroyal is an herb of protection, peace and strength. Cunningham notes that it is carried on board ships to prevent seasickness and for safe travel, given to quarrelling couples to end their fighting, and carried for strength and protection against the evil eye. It is also placed in the shoes for endurance during long walks, and used in business deals to bring success. Use it only in sealed sachets, by hanging dried sprigs, or as a living plant. Honour Demeter and the Eleusinian Mysteries with its image or a living pot rather than drinking it.
medicalUses: Historically, pennyroyal was used to repel fleas, to induce menstruation, and as a remedy for colds and digestive complaints. These internal uses are now known to be dangerous: pennyroyal oil has caused deaths, and even strong teas can damage the liver. Today it is only used externally as a living pest-repellent plant.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, it grows in damp grassland, along pond and ditch edges and in seasonally wet ground. It can be grown in moist, sunny spots in the garden, away from pets and children. Dried herb is occasionally sold for magical use; American pennyroyal (Hedeoma pulegioides) has the same toxic compound.
uses: Carry dried pennyroyal in a sealed sachet when travelling by sea for safe passage
Give a sealed sachet to a quarrelling couple to bring peace
Hang dried sprigs (out of reach) to repel fleas and evil
Tuck a sealed sachet into a briefcase for success in business
Grow a pot of pennyroyal in honour of Demeter
Place a sealed sachet in your bag for strength on long journeys
caution: POISONOUS: pennyroyal contains pulegone, which causes liver and kidney failure. Pennyroyal oil is deadly even in small amounts and has killed people who took it to end a pregnancy. Never ingest the oil, tea or herb, and do not apply the oil to skin. Keep away from children and pets, avoid all contact during pregnancy, and seek emergency help if any is swallowed.
pets: Toxic to dogs and cats; pennyroyal oil used as a flea treatment has killed pets. Never apply it to animals or let them chew the plant.

name: Lady's Mantle
description: A soft, low plant with pleated, scalloped leaves that catch morning dew in silvery beads, and froths of lime-green flowers. Medieval Christians named it for the cloak of the Virgin Mary, while earlier it may have been sacred to Freya. Alchemists gathered the dewdrops from its leaves, believing them the purest of waters for the Great Work. Its genus name Alchemilla means 'little alchemist'.
metaphysicalUses: Lady's mantle is an herb of love, women's mysteries and alchemical transformation. Its sachets and infusions are used in love spells, and it is considered sacred to goddesses of love, fertility and motherhood. The dew collected from its leaves at dawn, especially on May morning, was prized for magic and beauty. It is used for youth and beauty rituals, for moon water and in alchemical work toward transformation. It is used in rites of passage through women's lives: menarche, pregnancy blessings (symbolic only), motherhood and menopause, and in gentle protective charms for the home.
medicalUses: Lady's mantle was a favourite herb of medieval wise women. As an astringent and 'woman's herb', its tea was used to ease heavy menstrual bleeding and cramps, to tone the womb after childbirth, and for diarrhoea. Washes and compresses were used on wounds, skin sores and inflamed eyes, and gargles for sore throats and mouth ulcers.
whereToFind: Native to Europe, western Asia and Greenland, it grows in damp grassland, mountain meadows, woodland edges and along streams. Its relative Alchemilla mollis is a popular garden plant that grows easily in sun or part shade. Gather leaves in summer while flowering. Dried herb is sold by herb suppliers.
uses: Collect the dewdrops from its leaves at dawn on May morning for beauty magic
Add lady's mantle to a love sachet with rose
Use leaves in moon water for women's mysteries rituals
Brew a gentle tea for menstrual cramps
Hang a bundle in the home as a protective 'mantle'
Use in alchemical meditations on transformation
caution: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, as it may stimulate the uterus. Its tannins may upset sensitive stomachs and, in large amounts taken long-term, may strain the liver. Consult a healthcare provider before medicinal use, and see a doctor about heavy menstrual bleeding.
interactions: Tannins may reduce absorption of other medicines and iron; take them a couple of hours apart.

name: Motherwort
description: A tall, square-stemmed mint-family plant with jagged, lion-paw leaves and tiers of small pink flowers set in prickly whorls. Its species name 'cardiaca' means 'of the heart'. Since the days of the ancient Greeks it has been used for anxious, heavy hearts and the trials of motherhood. Culpeper wrote that there is no better herb 'to drive melancholy vapours from the heart'.
metaphysicalUses: Motherwort is an herb of protection, courage and the heart. It is used for spells of maternal protection, motherhood and family blessing, and to nurture self-love and inner strength. It soothes grief and anxiety in rituals of emotional healing. Its lion-like leaves make it an ally for confidence and courage, and old lore says it brings long life. Hang it in the home for protection, add it to self-love baths and charms, or plant it in the garden as a guardian of mothers and children.
medicalUses: In Western herbalism, motherwort is a classic heart and nerve herb. Its bitter tea or tincture was used to calm anxiety, nervous palpitations, tension and irritability, to ease menstrual cramps and delayed periods, and to steady women through menopause and its hot flushes and mood changes. It was traditionally given after childbirth to help the womb recover.
whereToFind: Native to central Asia and southeastern Europe, it is widely naturalised along roadsides, hedgerows, waste places and old gardens. It is a hardy perennial and very easy to grow, often self-seeding. Harvest flowering tops in summer, wearing gloves against the prickly calyces. Dried herb and tinctures are sold by herb suppliers.
uses: Add motherwort to a self-love bath to nurture the heart
Hang a bundle over the cradle or nursery door for maternal protection
Carry a sachet for courage and confidence
Plant motherwort in the garden as a guardian of mothers and children
Take a few drops of tincture in water for anxiety, with a healthcare provider's approval
Use in emotional healing rituals after grief or heartbreak
caution: Do not use during pregnancy, as it stimulates the uterus and may cause miscarriage; avoid while breastfeeding. Avoid with heavy menstrual bleeding. May cause drowsiness, diarrhea or stomach upset. Can cause skin sensitivity in sunlight in some people. Consult a healthcare provider before use, especially with heart conditions, and stop 2 weeks before surgery.
interactions: May add to the effects of sedatives and alcohol. Use caution with heart medicines (such as digoxin) and blood thinners.

name: Sweetgrass
description: A fragrant grass of northern meadows and wetlands whose leaves smell of vanilla and fresh hay, thanks to coumarin. For many Indigenous nations of North America it is one of the four sacred medicines, the hair of Mother Earth, braided in three strands for mind, body and spirit. In Europe it was strewn before church doors on saints' days, giving it the name 'holy grass', and flavours Polish bison-grass vodka.
metaphysicalUses: Sweetgrass is a sacred medicine used to attract positive energy and kindly spirits. In many Indigenous traditions, after burning sage to cleanse, a braid of sweetgrass is lit and the smoke is wafted to bring in blessings and good spirits. Sweetgrass belongs to those living cultures, so respect it by buying from Indigenous harvesters and learning its protocols rather than appropriating ceremonies. In folk practice a braid can be hung in the home for peace and blessing, placed on an ancestor altar, or used in gratitude rituals. Its sweet scent invites calm, kindness and gentleness.
medicalUses: Some Indigenous nations traditionally used sweetgrass tea or washes for colds, coughs, sore throats and windburn. Because sweetgrass contains coumarin, which can affect the liver and blood clotting, internal use is not recommended outside traditional, knowledgeable guidance.
whereToFind: Native across the northern parts of North America, Europe and Asia, it grows in wet meadows, lake shores, prairies and marsh edges. It can be grown from plugs in moist, sunny garden beds and spreads by runners. Cut blades in early to midsummer. Braids are best bought directly from Indigenous artisans and harvesters, or from reputable native-owned shops.
uses: Hang a sweetgrass braid in the home to invite peace and good spirits
Place a braid on an ancestor altar as an offering of gratitude
Gently burn the end of a braid after cleansing to bring in blessings
Tuck a few blades into a blessing sachet for a new home
Grow sweetgrass in a damp garden bed as a gift to the land
Buy braids directly from Indigenous makers as an act of respect
caution: Contains coumarin, which can harm the liver and may affect blood clotting if taken internally; do not consume it outside knowledgeable traditional guidance, and avoid with blood thinners, liver disease or during pregnancy. When burning a braid, use a fireproof dish, keep it away from flammables, never leave it unattended, and ventilate the room. Respect the cultural protocols of the Indigenous nations to whom it is sacred.
interactions: Internal use may add to the effects of blood thinners such as warfarin.
pets: Keep smoke and braids away from pets and birds.

name: Hibiscus
description: A tropical mallow whose fleshy, ruby-red calyces make a tart, crimson drink loved across the world: agua de Jamaica in Mexico, sorrel at Caribbean Christmas, karkadé in Egypt and bissap in West Africa. Its sister, the showy Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, is offered to the goddess Kali and to Ganesha in India. In Polynesian lore a hibiscus behind the ear tells the world whether one's heart is free.
metaphysicalUses: Hibiscus is a flower of love, lust and divination. Cunningham notes that in tropical lands a brew of hibiscus was drunk for its lust-inducing powers, and that the flowers were added to love incenses and sachets. Hibiscus also features in divination and dream magic. Its blood-red infusion is offered to Kali, and in some traditions to Oshun, and is used as a substitute for wine or blood in ritual. Drink it to awaken passion, use the brew as a scrying liquid, or add it to beauty and glamour baths.
medicalUses: Across Africa, Asia and the Americas, hibiscus tea is a cooling, tart folk remedy for fevers, colds, mild digestive upsets and as a gentle diuretic. Modern studies suggest that regular hibiscus tea may help lower mildly raised blood pressure. It is rich in vitamin C and antioxidants and was used to support the liver.
whereToFind: Native to tropical Africa and widely cultivated in warm countries, it grows as an annual shrub in full sun and warm soil. It can be grown from seed in warm summers or greenhouses. Harvest calyces when plump and red. Dried 'flor de Jamaica' is sold at Mexican, Caribbean and Middle Eastern groceries, tea shops and herb suppliers.
uses: Brew a crimson hibiscus tea to share with a lover to awaken passion
Use the deep red infusion as a scrying liquid in a black bowl
Offer hibiscus flowers to Kali on her festival days
Add dried hibiscus to love incense and sachets
Use hibiscus tea as a substitute for wine or blood in ritual
Float the flowers in a glamour bath for beauty
caution: Generally safe in food amounts. It may lower blood pressure and blood sugar; use caution with blood pressure and diabetes medicines. Avoid medicinal amounts during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Consult a healthcare provider if you take prescription medicines.
interactions: May add to blood pressure medicines (including hydrochlorothiazide and losartan) and diabetes medicines. May lower levels of chloroquine and simvastatin, alter acetaminophen handling, and increase side effects of erlotinib.

name: Saffron
description: The crimson threads from the heart of a lilac autumn crocus, each flower yielding only three, so that a pound of spice needs some 75,000 blossoms. This makes it the world's most precious spice. Minoan frescoes show women gathering it. Cleopatra was said to bathe in saffron for beauty, and the Greeks scattered it in halls and theatres. In myth, it sprang from the blood of the youth Crocus, beloved of Hermes.
metaphysicalUses: Saffron is a precious solar herb of love, happiness and strength. Cunningham notes it is used in love and healing charms, and that it raises the spirits and elevates happiness. In ancient Persia, saffron water was used to raise the wind, and drinking saffron tea was thought to induce clairvoyance and psychic powers. It is used to bless and consecrate, and in Hindu ritual, kesar paste marks the brow of devotees. A single thread offered on the altar is a gift worthy of the gods, and it can dye ritual cloth, ink and bread a solar gold for sun magic and abundance.
medicalUses: In Persian, Ayurvedic and European folk medicine, saffron has been used to lift the spirits and ease melancholy, to calm anxiety, to relieve menstrual cramps and PMS, and to aid digestion. Modern studies suggest it may help mild to moderate depression. Culinary amounts are safe; medicinal amounts should be guided by a professional.
whereToFind: Probably originating in Greece and southwest Asia, it is now grown chiefly in Iran, Spain, Kashmir, Greece and Morocco. Corms can be planted in late summer in sunny, well-drained soil for autumn flowers; pick the red stigmas by hand on the morning they open. Buy saffron threads from reputable spice merchants and grocers, since fakes are common. Never confuse saffron crocus with the deadly autumn crocus (Colchicum).
uses: Offer a single saffron thread on the altar as a precious gift to the gods
Steep saffron in water to make a golden ink for writing love spells
Bake saffron bread or rice to bless a family celebration with happiness
Add a few threads to a love charm bag
Paint a golden kesar mark on your brow in solar rituals
Sip a little saffron tea before divination
caution: Safe in culinary amounts (up to about 1.5 g a day). Doses of about 5 g are toxic and can cause severe bleeding, and 10 to 20 g can be fatal. Avoid medicinal doses during pregnancy, as it can stimulate the uterus, and avoid with bleeding disorders. Do not confuse it with the poisonous autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale), which looks similar.
interactions: May increase bleeding risk with blood thinners and antiplatelet drugs (such as rivaroxaban, warfarin, aspirin). Medicinal doses may add to antidepressants and blood pressure medicines.
pets: Keep the bulbs away from pets; autumn crocus (the look-alike) is highly toxic to dogs and cats.

name: Lemon Verbena
description: A graceful South American shrub whose slender leaves release a bright, clean lemon scent at the lightest touch. Spanish explorers brought it to Europe in the seventeenth century and named it after Princess Maria Luisa of Parma. It became a favourite of Victorian ladies, who tucked its leaves into handkerchiefs. In Gone with the Wind, Scarlett O'Hara's mother always smells of lemon verbena.
metaphysicalUses: Lemon verbena is an herb of purification and love. Cunningham notes that it is worn to make one attractive to the opposite sex, and that it is used in purification and love spells. It is said to make dreams more pleasant and to break bad dreams when worn around the neck or placed under the pillow. Add it to cleansing baths and floor washes for a bright, clarifying energy, to love sachets, and to spells for beauty and charm. Its sunny scent lifts a heavy mood and clears the mind.
medicalUses: In South American and European folk herbalism, lemon verbena tea ('verveine' or 'cedrón') is a favourite after-dinner digestive. It is used to ease indigestion, bloating and cramping, to soothe nervous tension and to help with sleep. It was also used as a mild fever remedy and for colds.
whereToFind: Native to Argentina, Chile, Peru and other parts of South America, it grows as a woody shrub in warm climates. It is frost-tender, so grow it in a pot in full sun and bring it indoors for winter in cold climates. Harvest leaves throughout summer. Plants are found at garden centers and herb nurseries; dried leaves at tea shops and herb suppliers.
uses: Wear a lemon verbena leaf in a locket to attract love
Place a sprig under the pillow to drive away bad dreams
Add lemon verbena to a purification bath
Brew an after-dinner tea for digestion and calm
Use in a floor wash to clear stagnant energy and bring brightness
Tuck leaves into letters and love notes
caution: Generally safe as a tea. May irritate the kidneys in large or long-term amounts; avoid with kidney disease. Avoid medicinal amounts during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The essential oil can cause skin sensitization and photosensitivity and is banned as a fragrance ingredient, so do not apply it to skin. Do not confuse with vervain (Verbena officinalis).
pets: The ASPCA lists lemon verbena as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (digestive upset, colic), mainly from its essential oils.

name: Borage
description: A bristly, cucumber-scented annual with nodding, star-shaped flowers of brilliant sky blue, adored by bees. Its old saying is 'I, Borage, bring always courage', and Roman soldiers and medieval knights drank borage in wine before battle. Ladies embroidered its flowers on the scarves of crusaders. Pliny wrote that it 'maketh a man merry and joyful', and the herb of gladness has graced summer drinks ever since.
metaphysicalUses: Borage is an herb of courage and gladness. Cunningham notes that carrying the fresh flowers gives courage, especially when walking outdoors, and that borage tea induces psychic powers. Use it in spells for confidence and strength before any challenge. Float the star-shaped flowers in drinks to bring joy to gatherings and banish melancholy. Its blue stars are also used in protection charms and in rites to Jupiter, for joy, generosity and expansion. Plant it to bring bees and happiness into the garden.
medicalUses: Traditional herbals praised borage to 'comfort the heart' and drive away sorrow. Folk healers used it for fevers, coughs and as a cooling remedy, and its leaves in poultices for inflammations. Today, borage seed oil, rich in gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), is taken as a supplement for skin conditions like eczema, inflammatory joint complaints and menopausal symptoms.
whereToFind: Native to the Mediterranean, it is now grown in gardens worldwide and naturalised in waste places. It is an easy, self-seeding annual for sunny, well-drained soil, flowering from early summer to frost. Pick flowers fresh in the morning. Seeds and plants are found at garden centers; borage seed oil capsules at health food stores.
uses: Carry fresh borage flowers for courage before a challenge
Float borage stars in summer drinks to bring gladness to a gathering
Freeze flowers in ice cubes for festive midsummer punches
Sip borage tea (occasionally) before psychic work
Plant borage to bring bees and joy to the garden
Add dried flowers to a confidence charm bag
caution: Borage leaves, flowers and seeds contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can harm the liver; eat flowers only occasionally as a garnish, and avoid regular or medicinal use of the leaves. Use only certified PA-free borage seed oil. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, in children, and with liver disease or bleeding disorders. Borage seed oil has been linked to seizures, so avoid it with epilepsy. Consult a healthcare provider.
interactions: Seed oil (GLA) may increase bleeding with blood thinners and may raise seizure risk with drugs that lower the seizure threshold (such as phenothiazines). Avoid with other drugs that can harm the liver.
pets: The ASPCA lists borage as toxic to dogs, cats and horses (vomiting, diarrhea, skin irritation).
